pending_diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS: Acute Intermittent Porphyria (AIP) THE SMOKING GUN: The triad of severe neurovisceral abdominal pain without peritoneal signs, SIADH-induced hyponatremia triggered by fasting and sulfa drugs, and urine turning port-wine colored upon oxidation by ambient light. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: AIP is an autosomal dominant inborn error of heme biosynthesis caused by a partial deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD/HMBS). Stressors such as caloric restriction (fasting) and CYP450-inducing medications (sulfonamides, haloperidol, metoclopramide) upregulate hepatic delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase 1 (ALAS1). This drives the massive accumulation and systemic circulation of neurotoxic heme precursors: delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG). These precursors induce autonomic neuropathy (severe hypertension, tachycardia, gut dysmotility mimicking an acute abdomen), central neurotoxicity (psychosis, seizures, hypothalamic damage causing SIADH), and severe peripheral motor axonopathy (ascending paralysis, wrist drop). PBG oxidizes on light exposure to porphobilin, rendering the urine dark red or port-wine colored. Treatment requires immediate cessation of offending xenobiotics, high-dose intravenous glucose/dextrose, and IV hemin to downregulate ALAS1 via negative feedback.
